item.title: Houthis deny report that they attacked Mecca and Medina
item.description:
Houthis deny report that they attacked Mecca and Medina

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis denied on Saturday Saudi Arabia's report that they attacked the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, after Riyadh said it had intercepted Houthi missiles headed towards the two cities.

The group said its operations target Saudi oil facilities and military bases, and that it announces such attacks when they occur.

item.title: Iran judiciary says chief holds rare meeting with supreme leader
item.description:
Iran judiciary says chief holds rare meeting with supreme leader

Iran's judiciary said on Saturday that its chief held a rare meeting with the country's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who has yet to appear in public since being appointed.

Mojtaba was chosen in March to succeed his father and longtime ruler Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was killed in US-Israeli strikes in central Tehran alongside senior military commanders at the start of the Middle East war, and was said to have been injured in the same attack.

Judiciary chief Gholamhossein Mohseni Ejei and the supreme leader discussed issues including "securing public rights, and effectively combating corruption and its bottlenecks", the judiciary's Mizan Online website reported.

They held talks on "pursuing the recovery of rights and compensation for material and moral damages arising from the crimes of American-Zionist criminals", it said.

item.title: US envoy accuses Druze sheikh of using its backing to persecute other members of the community
item.description:
US envoy accuses Druze sheikh of using its backing to persecute other members of the community

US envoy Tom Barrack has criticised a prominent Druze leader in southern Syria, accusing him of exploiting the perception of Israeli backing and US support to persecute other members of the community.

Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria, made the remarks in an interview with the commentator Mario Nawfal published on X on Friday.

Barrack said his concern was not Israel but “a particular Druze sheikh”, whom he accused of using perceived Israeli backing and an apparent alignment with Washington to persecute other Druze.

“But let me tell you what, it’s not Israel that worries me. It’s a particular Druze sheikh who utilises the perception of Israeli backing and some alignment with America to persecute other Druze”.

Read more: US envoy accuses Druze sheikh of using its backing to persecute other members of the community

item.title: US envoy accuses Druze sheikh of using its backing to persecute other members of the community
item.description:
US envoy accuses Druze sheikh of using its backing to persecute other members of the community

Submitted by Reem Aouir on Sat, 10/24/2026 - 17:05
Tom Barrack says Sweida 'lives off' the captagon trade and that Israel and Syria 'will come to terms'
US ambassador to Turkey, Tom Barrack, during a press conference following the Nato summit in Ankara on 8 July 2026 (Altan Gocher/Hans Lucas via Reuters Connect)
Off

US envoy Tom Barrack has criticised a prominent Druze leader in southern Syria, accusing him of exploiting the perception of Israeli backing and US support to persecute other members of the community.

Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria, made the remarks in an interview with the commentator Mario Nawfal published on X on Friday.

Barrack said his concern was not Israel but “a particular Druze sheikh”, whom he accused of using perceived Israeli backing and an apparent alignment with Washington to persecute other Druze.

“But let me tell you what, it’s not Israel that worries me. It’s a particular Druze sheikh who utilises the perception of Israeli backing and some alignment with America to persecute other Druze”.

Barrack did not name the sheikh in the remarks. However, his comments come amid tensions surrounding Hikmat al-Hijri, a prominent Druze spiritual leader in Sweida who opposes Damascus's authority, called for Israeli support and advocated for independence from Syria.

Barrack further rejected the claims suggesting the sheikh had Washington's support, saying “it's absolutely wrong".

Earlier this month, Hijri's supporters raised Israeli flags at a rally in Sweida marking the anniversary of the 7 October 2023 attack.

Barrack also indicated that the armed Druze factions in the province are funding their weapons through the captagon trade.

"Sweida to Daraa is the captagon manufacturing operation of the world. That's what it does. It lives off of the manufacturing and selling of illicit drugs," he said.

"The Druze can arm themselves with the money that they're making from the captagon trade. This captagon is something, and it's like manufacturing meth," he added.

However, the "Bashan administration", affiliated with al-Hijri, rejected Barrack's statements and denied that Jabal Bashan is a centre for captagon production in a Facebook post.

“The Bashan administration expresses its profound anger and unequivocal condemnation of the misleading falsehoods and baseless accusations made by US Presidential Special Envoy Tom Barrack in his recent remarks.

"We categorically reject Barrack's reckless attempt to portray Jabal Bashan as a centre for captagon production. It is a matter of public record that our community stood on the front lines against smuggling networks, confronting them at great personal cost and sacrificing some of its finest young men in the struggle to eradicate this scourge," the statement read.

In May 2026, al-Hijri declared that the move toward self-determination cannot be reversed, emphasising the goal of creating a fully independent administration for Jabal Bashan, entirely distinct from Damascus's government.

Regarding Israel's relationship with the Druze, Barrack said the relationship was beyond political interference, pointing to Druze communities in the Golan Heights and along the border.

“Israel’s alignment with the Druze is not just for political interference. The Druze, the Golan Heights Druze and the Druze right on the border have paid the price of being an ally along with the IDF soldiers forever.”

Israel has repeatedly presented its military intervention in southern Syria as an effort to protect the Druze, and in July 2025 it struck Syrian government forces during the fighting in Sweida.

Barrack said Syria had exercised restraint in response to Israeli incursions, warning that retaliation could trigger a wider conflict.

"Syria has been very cautious. It knows that if it bites on one of these incursions, the fire is going to explode."

"So it's been very patient in allowing Israel to protect its 'buffer zone' by coming across and having the Druze conduct themselves inappropriately," he added.

Syria and Israel expected to reach understanding

On relations between Damascus and Tel Aviv, Barrack said he believed the two countries would eventually reach an understanding, despite continuing mistrust and tensions along their shared border.

“I think Israel and Syria will come to terms,” he said, arguing that Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa had made clear he did not want a confrontation with Israel.

U.S. Ambassador to Türkiye Tom Barrack on Syria:

I think Israel and Syria will come to terms, because President al-Sharaa has been very clear of saying, "I have no predatory interest to you, and I want to calm these waters."

And al-Sharaa doesn't have a Hezbollah, he hasn't… pic.twitter.com/P6rHngSko6

— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 23, 2026

He said Israel remained wary of Syria's new leadership because of Sharaa's past as a fighter with al-Nusra Front and the presence of foreign fighters in Syrian army divisions deployed near the Israeli border.

Barrack said Israel was seeking greater security along its border following the Hamas-led attacks of 7 October 2023, adding that Israeli officials remained unconvinced that Syria's assurances were sufficient.

Barrack described the negotiations between Syria and Israel as an ongoing trust-building process, saying the two sides have held five rounds of border and boundary talks, beginning in Paris in May 2024.

“We almost got there. I think we'll get there again,” he said.

item.title: Yemen's Houthis say they attacked Saudi oil facilities, airports
item.description:
Yemen's Houthis say they attacked Saudi oil facilities, airports

Yemen's Houthi group said it launched attacks at Saudi oil facilities and airports on Saturday including a Saudi Aramco facility in Yanbu, the Rabigh oil refinery and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh.

The group's military spokesperson, Yahya Saree, said it also targeted King Fahd International Airport in Dammam as well as Najran airport and an air base in Khamis Mushait.

There was no immediate confirmation from Saudi authorities.

Yemen's Houthis claim attack on Aden naval base, military camp

Yemen's Houthis claimed an attack on Saturday on a naval base and a military camp in Aden, the interim seat of the internationally recognised government, after blasts were heard there.

"Our armed forced targeted Saudi enemy concentrations at the so-called Al-Nasr camp and the naval base in Aden," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said, adding that the sites were overseen by Saudi forces.

Reporting by AFP

Houthis say Saudi strike kills five members of same family in Hodeida

Reporting by AFP

item.description:
Explosions heard in Yemen's city of Aden

Explosions were heard on Saturday in Aden, a city in the south of the country that serves as the seat of the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, according to a police source and an AFP journalist.

item.title: After deadly shooting, Israel forcibly evicts hundreds of Palestinian families from Hebron homes
item.description:
After deadly shooting, Israel forcibly evicts hundreds of Palestinian families from Hebron homes

Submitted by Fayha Shalash on Sat, 10/24/2026 - 12:38
Residents say soldiers gave families five minutes to leave, as demolitions accompany an Israeli military operation that officials warn could trigger a crisis
Higazi Shawer Al Tamimi, 70, who was displaced with his family from the Ein Deir Baha neighbourhood by Israeli forces, inside his animal feed shop in Hebron, occupied West Bank, 24 October 2026 (John Wessels/AFP)
Off

Israeli forces have forcibly evicted hundreds of Palestinian families from their homes across several neighbourhoods after a shooting on Friday near the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint west of Hebron, in which two soldiers were killed and three others wounded.

As part of what it termed an "operation to thwart terrorism",  the Israeli military said the operation was launched in the city of Hebron, in coordination with the Shin Bet (internal security service) and the Border Police in the West Bank.

The two suspected Palestinian attackers were also killed by Israeli forces, according to the military. 

The army said it was conducting searches to locate and dismantle what it described as “terrorist infrastructure” and weapons, while interrogating dozens of suspects.

It said the operation was focused on the area from which the alleged attackers had operated and that residents could leave through designated exits. 

But residents described being ordered from their homes at gunpoint, with little time to gather belongings and no clear information about when they would be allowed to return.

The families who spoke to Middle East Eye said they were evicted on Saturday morning from the neighbourhoods of al-Jalada, Ein Deir Bahha, Wadi al-Maghariba and Shi'b al-Milh.

The al-Jalada neighbourhood is home to the families of the two alleged perpetrators of the shooting, Ahmad and Hamouda al-Joba, who were killed by Israeli military fire after they reportedly killed two soldiers and wounded others.

Abdul Hamid Shahada, a resident in the neighbourhood, told MEE that the Israeli military stormed the area shortly after the attack on Friday morning.

A large number of soldiers, accompanied by several military vehicles, took up positions near the homes of the Joba family.

During the incursion, the Israeli military distributed a map designating homes and adjacent buildings for evacuation and compelled a number of families to leave their residences.

'Until further notice'    

Shahada and his family said they watched the unfolding events from their windows.

“We watched them forcing families out of their homes; they even beat one of the men."

"We stayed in our building, waiting anxiously, and packed small bags with essentials: medicines, mobile phone chargers, and important documents. We didn't sleep all night," he said.

Death, displacement and disease: A young Gaza doctor on life under Israeli bombardment
Read More »

At 9am on Saturday, soldiers stormed the family’s building and ordered Shahada to tell all the residents, about 54 people, mostly children, along with his 79-year-old ailing mother, to leave at once. 

"They gave us only five minutes. Although we had anticipated an evacuation and tried to prepare the children, they were trembling and crying. Even the women wept as we were being led out," he told MEE. 

"The soldiers ordered us to keep our hands behind our heads and forbade us from taking any clothing or belongings other than our small personal bags," he added.

The soldiers directed the families along a specific route toward Al-Salam Street.

From there, some went to stay with relatives, while others sought shelter at the Child Happiness Centre, which the municipality had opened to accommodate them.

The soldiers didn’t tell Shahada and his family when they might be able to return, saying only "until further notice", though they did inform some other families that they would be kept out of their homes for six months to a year.

Shahada and his family say they cannot stop thinking about the fate of their homes, especially after seeing the houses of their neighbours left with doors and windows wide open and being ransacked and vandalised by the soldiers.

Emergency plan  

The forcible displacement has coincided with demolitions targeting residential buildings, commercial shops and industrial facilities in Farsh al-Hawa, west of Hebron. Local sources reported that around seven dunums of land had been levelled. 

Israeli forces also imposed a broad closure on the city of Hebron and its surrounding villages, towns and refugee camps, blocking main entrances and roads. Simultaneously, they raided homes, conducted searches and carried out arrests. 

Gaza genocide leaves record number of orphans and widows
Read More »

Local sources reported that at least 13 Palestinians were arrested in the city, while dozens were detained for several hours and subjected to field interrogations.

In response to the repercussions of the operation, the Hebron Municipality announced the activation of an emergency plan.

This includes the preparation of shelters for families forced to leave their homes, as well as the establishment of an operations centre to monitor residents' needs amid concerns that the scope of evacuations may expand and the number of families requiring shelter could rise.

Khaled al-Qawasmi, deputy mayor of Hebron, told MEE that the Israeli military began its operation in the area around midnight, giving residents one hour to vacate their homes.

He said that the evacuation included both adults and children, and that residents were not permitted to remain in the area.

Approximately 250 families have been forced to leave the area so far, Qawasmi said, noting that this figure is not final, given the ongoing military siege and the possibility that more families may be evacuated. 

"Families evacuated during the first wave sought refuge in the homes of relatives, while the Hebron Municipality worked to open centres to accommodate those affected, including family guesthouses, the Childhood Happiness Centre, the Korean Centre and several other facilities," he said.

Qawasmi warned that if the military operation continues and expands, it could lead to a crisis in finding shelter, given the limited capacity of the centres already opened to accommodate any additional people.

"The military operation has not ended, and the closure is not limited to the targeted area; it extends to the entrances and gateways of Hebron, with Israeli forces continuing to be deployed across various parts of the city," he said.

Death toll from Jordan church attack rises to nine

item.title: In Athens, Marco Rubio's civilisational hubris reaches a peak
item.description:
In Athens, Marco Rubio's civilisational hubris reaches a peak

Submitted by Marco Carnelos on Thu, 10/22/2026 - 21:02
The US secretary of state holds up a flattering mirror to the West, ignoring centuries of catastrophic imperialism
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio speaks in Athens, Greece, on 7 October 2026 (Mark Schiefelbein/AFP)
Off

On 7 October, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered a remarkable speech in Athens. The event did not produce significant headlines - but it should have. 

Rubio’s statement deserves scrutiny, both because he could be a contender for the Republican nomination ahead of the 2028 presidential elections, and for the problematic nature of his comments (to say the least).

Standing before the Parthenon, he delivered less a speech than a sermon on civilisational destiny. 

Rubio told his Athenian audience that the West owes the world its curiosity, its ambition, its “impatience with the notion of impossibility”. The setting was magnificent, and the rhetoric was built to match. 

Unfortunately, it was nothing more than an exercise in selective memory and civilisational vanity.

Rubio’s central claim was that the ancient Greeks gave rise to traits that “would come to define the West”, setting it apart from “so many other cultures and civilisations where stability and subsistence were the highest ends of life”.

This sentence deserves close attention. It essentially describes the builders of Cambodia’s Angkor temples, the astronomers of Samarkand, the engineers of the Inca road system, and the mathematicians of India’s Kerala as people who aimed for subsistence.

It ignores Ibn Battuta, who spent three decades crossing the known world, longer than Marco Polo’s journey. It overlooks the Polynesian navigators who settled the Pacific with no instruments. The list could go on and on.

History of subjugation

It is also a strange reading of the Greeks themselves. Rubio praised Herodotus-style curiosity as a western trait, yet much of what reached medieval Europe from Greek philosophy and science survived because Baghdad’s Islamic scholars translated, preserved and extended it. 

The “unbroken” western inheritance he described ran through Arab-Islamic libraries and Muslim Spain. A civilisation that borrows, adapts, and is rescued by others is the normal human story - not a lineage of lone exceptionalism.

Rubio presented Alexander the Great, Caesar, Charlemagne and Cortes as bearers of one noble flame, hailing “the qualities that led Alexander to conquer the entire known world”. 

The western science and cartography Rubio celebrates were instruments of conquest, used to chart coasts, classify peoples and justify hierarchies

Cortes, we should remember, destroyed the Aztec capital and subjugated millions. Columbus, who Rubio credited with “discovery”, began a system of forced labour and enslavement on Hispaniola that devastated the native population within a generation.

The same restless hunger “to know the mysteries” and “chafe at all boundaries” drove the Atlantic slave trade, in which roughly 12 million Africans were forced onto ships; well over a million died in the crossing. 

It also drove the partition of Africa at the Berlin Conference in 1884-85; the Opium Wars in the mid-19th century, where the United Kingdom forced narcotics on China at gunpoint; and the devastation of India and Belgian King Leopold’s Congo, where rubber quotas were enforced with mutilation, and millions died. 

The western science and cartography Rubio celebrates were instruments of conquest, used to chart coasts, classify peoples and justify hierarchies.

Rubio spoke of “daring exploration and invention”, as though the word “exploration” required no further comment. For those on the receiving end, exploration was frequently the first stage of invasion. 

A speech that celebrates ambition, but never counts the costs, is not history; it is advertising.

Rhetorical trap

The venue itself undermined Rubio’s argument. The Athens of Pericles, the golden age Rubio invoked, ran on slavery. Enslaved people made up a large share of Attica’s population, working the silver mines at Laurion, in conditions that few survived. Women and foreigners were excluded from citizenship. The democracy Rubio admires was a democracy of a minority of adult men.

The speech’s most revealing passage was his diagnosis of the contemporary West. Rubio argued that the West lost its thumos, its fire, because it became “ashamed of the very things that made us exceptional”. 

Prosperity became “a source of guilt”. Countries “opened our borders and outsourced our industry”, and surrendered sovereignty to “global bureaucracies”.

For the record, the country that in the 20th century advocated more than anyone else a policy of “open borders” was the US itself. This same country outsourced its industry abroad for greed, increasing profits by reducing labour costs and throwing US blue-collar workers under the bus. 

Rubio turns historical scholarship into weakness. In his view, those who study the slave trade, colonial violence or the dispossession of Native Americans are participants in civilisational decline - people who have lost the will to survive. 

This is a rhetorical trap. It makes honest accounting unpatriotic, and leaves only celebration.

Meanwhile, Rubio described the US itself as an “open and wild land” that became the site of a “great revival of western imagination”, noting that the Greek aspiration for new horizons “became the American frontier spirit”. 

Once again, for the record, that land was neither open nor empty. It was inhabited by hundreds of indigenous tribes, who were displaced, killed or confined into reserves through treaties broken as quickly as they were signed. Rubio’s speech was the old language of manifest destiny, polished for a new audience.

He then added that this tradition “transformed an infant seaboard republic into a continental empire” - the last word uttered without apparent unease, even approvingly. That word choice, from a State Department that claims to oppose imperial ambitions elsewhere, deserves attention.

Flaw that brought down kings

Finally, there is the contrast Rubio draws with Iran, whose leaders, he said, worship death, while “our heroes do not”. It is a comfortable line that conveniently forgets how often western powers have glorified sacrifice for flag and empire. 

The slaughter of 1914 was sold to young Europeans in precisely these terms of duty, honour and glory. The cult of heroic death is hardly foreign to the West. Pretending otherwise requires forgetting the First World War entirely.

The Greeks had a word for what Rubio’s speech displayed: hubris, the arrogance of the powerful who mistake fortune for virtue. Their tragedians returned to it obsessively. It was the flaw that brought down kings who believed their success proved their superiority. 

Rubio declared a return to brutal western colonialism - and Europe applauded
Read More »

The play Persians by Aeschylus, performed eight years after the Battle of Salamis, depicts the fall of the Persian emperor Xerxes as a warning to the victors, not a taunt to the defeated.

A speech delivered at the symbol of Greek history could have honoured that tradition. It could have said that the western inheritance is a mixture of brilliance and brutality; that curiosity without humility leads to catastrophe; and that the best use of the past is to learn from its failures. Instead, Rubio offered a flattering mirror. 

The intention here is not to deny the numerous outstanding achievements of western civilisation, beginning with the very tools of self-critique now used against it, or its role in the abolition of slavery and in the promotion of human rights law, science and human progress - but rather to place them in the right context, to avoid the mistaken belief that there is no alternative, or, as Rubio’s poor choice of words suggests, that there must not be.

The civilisation that the US secretary of state, and - God forbid - potentially next US president, described in his speech never actually existed. The one that did, with its conquests, slave ships and genuine achievements, deserves a more honest steward.

item.title: More than 1,500 Palestinians driven from homes in Hebron since Friday
item.description:
More than 1,500 Palestinians driven from homes in Hebron since Friday

The governor of Hebron has called for international intervention after around 1,500 Palestinians were forced from their homes in the occupied West Bank.

According to the Wafa news agency, Israeli forces since Friday have driven hundreds of people from their homes in the Deir Bahha and al-Jalda areas of Hebron.

More than 200 families have been left homeless as a result.

Hebron Governor Khaled Dudin told Wafa that the Israelis had plans to force out 2,500 further people in the coming hours.

item.title: Pakistan ratifies Mecca pact as Saudi Arabia faces attacks and Israel holds military drills
item.description:
Pakistan ratifies Mecca pact as Saudi Arabia faces attacks and Israel holds military drills

Submitted by MEE staff on Sat, 10/24/2026 - 10:25
Saudi authorities have lifted recent security alerts, while Washington signals the possibility of military action against Tehran
A man takes a picture of a billboard featuring Pakistan's Army Chief General Syed Asim Munir (C), Naval Chief Admiral Naveed Ashraf (R) and Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Babar Sidhu in Peshawar, 15 May 2025 (Abdul Majeed/AFP)
Off

Pakistan on Friday announced that it has ratified a joint defence pact with Turkey and Saudi Arabia as the kingdom faces renewed security threats and is looking for allies to help it against Yemen's Houthis. 

Pakistan’s Foreign Office spokesperson, Sajjad Haider Khan, said that Islamabad and Riyadh have completed their ratification procedures for the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed by the three countries on 7 August.

“Matters related to the agreement, its ratification, and operationalisation remain under discussion by the three parties,” Khan said, according to a transcript published by Pakistan’s Foreign Office.

Turkey is still completing its domestic approval process as the agreement has not yet completed ratification by all three signatories.

The pact was signed in Mecca by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Saudi Arabia's Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman. 

It provides for collective defence in the event of an external armed attack against any of the three countries, with the nature and level of assistance to be determined according to the circumstances.

The agreement has moved towards implementation following a 5 October meeting of the countries’ Strategic Political and Defence Committee.

Full text of the Mecca defence pact
Read More »

The meeting called for the implementation of collective defence commitments and the rapid deployment of military forces and capabilities in Saudi Arabia, subject to the countries’ domestic laws.

Islamabad has called the agreement defensive and consistent with the UN Charter.

The development comes amid growing fears of a wider regional escalation, with the Houthis continuing attacks on Saudi Arabia and US and Israeli officials reportedly discussing renewed strikes on Iran months after the conflict between the countries and Tehran began.

Regional escalation 

Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defence issued warnings over potential danger in parts of the kingdom this week before subsequently announcing that they had passed.

The alerts covered areas in the southwest, such as Abha and Khamis Mushait, although authorities did not disclose the nature of the danger.

They advised residents to follow safety instructions and refrain from gathering or filming in the affected areas, according to Anadolu Agency.

The alerts came amid an escalation involving Houthi missile and drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabia.  

'Except Mecca and Medina': Chaos across Saudi airports as Houthis claim Riyadh strikes
Read More »

On 21 October, Reuters reported that Riyadh’s allies were providing primarily defensive support as the kingdom sought to protect its infrastructure amid the threat of further attacks.

Meanwhile, the Israeli military has announced large-scale exercises in the north and central regions of Israel on Sunday and Monday, rehearsing scenarios relating to surprise attacks and infiltrations by air and land.

The exercises will involve the air force and units from the Northern and Central Commands of the military.

The military said the drills would test its readiness to defend against attacks on multiple fronts and prepare for any potential escalation along Israel’s borders.

The preparations come as Washington and Tel Aviv are reportedly considering renewed military action against Iran.

On Friday, Trump said that the US might conduct another military operation against Iran, as the conflict approached its eighth month.

American and Israeli militaries have already developed plans for renewed strikes following the US midterm elections on 3 November, a report published this week by The Business Times, citing US officials, said. 

The report said that potential targets could include Iranian energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and missile and drone capabilities.

item.title: Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi ballistic missiles fired towards Yanbu and Taif
item.description:
Saudi-led coalition says it destroyed Houthi ballistic missiles fired towards Yanbu and Taif

A Saudi-led ​coalition fighting Yemen's ‌Houthis said it destroyed two ballistic missiles fired ​by the Iran-aligned ​group towards Taif and Yanbu on Saturday, as fighting between the sides continued.

Saudi Arabia's civil defence on Saturday briefly issued alerts warning of potential danger in Taif and Yanbu, as well as the holy city of Mecca and its second-largest city Jeddah.

The service issued notices around 10 minutes later, saying that the danger had passed.

Reporting by Reuters
